title: Schedule your repeated marketing data checks for an agent
summary: Trackingplan's CEO says users asked its AI debugger to handle over 80% of tracking alerts, and scheduled agent checks ended up doing an analyst's routine work.
agent_role: The agent investigated tracking alerts, reproduced broken pages in a browser and ran scheduled checks like release audits. People set priorities, reviewed findings and decided fixes.
outcome: The CEO reports users asked the AI debugger to handle more than 80% of alerts and said it saved them several hours a week.
what_they_did: Trackingplan's team built a copilot for marketing analysts on nao, an open-source analytics agent, linked to their tracking data. Everyone in the company used it daily. They noticed they kept typing the same checks, so they put those prompts on a schedule or triggered them when a new release appeared.
how_it_went: The CEO says the debugger found a changed currency code that broke one market's revenue in Google Analytics, and the customer fixed it within hours. Scheduled checks ended up doing much of an analyst's routine job.
worth_knowing: The same question could get two different answers. They say a precise description of each table and metric, plain code for fixed rules, and tests fixed it, not a better model.
prompt: Every weekday morning, check [your analytics tool] for problems from yesterday's site release: missing events, broken checkout tracking, or revenue that doesn't match [your backend sales report]. Use these definitions: [conversion definition], [date range rules], [which accounts may be summed]. For each issue, say what broke, where, the likely cause and a suggested fix. Show me a short report and don't change any settings without my approval.

curation.rationale: A founder's account of scheduling repeated analytics checks for an agent and using it to debug tracking alerts; real use with one concrete example, but largely a company product story.
